subtype: Approach: sharing pet duties fairly among siblings [Action]
passage:
Sunday. "It's your turn!" "No, yours!" Gurleen and Mahima both stood over the hamster cage while Bhuri sat in a dirty corner with an empty dish.
Monday. Mahima drew a calendar on the fridge: Gurleen on odd dates, Mahima on even ones, each date with feeding and cage cleaning. Each sister ticked her boxes in her own colour.
Two weeks later. Bhuri's cage was clean and the dish full. Nobody had shouted for days, and when Gurleen forgot once, the empty box told her at a glance.

qa.q: Which dates belonged to Gurleen on the calendar?
What were the sisters feeling on Sunday?
qa.a: Annoyed and defensive, since each said it was the other's turn.

qa.q: What could the sisters do when one of them is away, and why?
qa.a: They could swap days and mark it on the calendar, so Bhuri is still fed and neither sister feels cheated.

qa.q: What is it like for Bhuri on Sunday while the sisters argue?
qa.a: Bhuri sits in a dirty corner with an empty dish, so the hamster goes without care while they argue.

grounding: Two sisters take turns on alternate days to feed and clean the hamster cage, and mark a calendar to avoid arguments.

subtype: Approach: sharing pet duties fairly among siblings [Action]
passage: Children, you're fighting again over whose turn it is with the parrot? Sit. When I was a girl of ten and my sister Zohra was eight, our Abba brought home a hamster in a shoebox. For one whole week we quarrelled every day. "I fed him yesterday!" "No, I did!" Once he got fed twice, and once not at all. So Ammi hung a calendar next to the cage and gave us two pencils, red for me, green for Zohra. Odd dates were mine, even dates were hers. Food, fresh water, and clean the corner of the cage. When you finished, you put your colour on the date. After that, if anyone said "your turn", we just looked at the calendar. I, Farida, cannot remember one more fight about that hamster.

qa.q: How did young Farida feel during the week of quarrels?
qa.a: Farida felt cross and frustrated, sure of having fed the hamster when Zohra said otherwise.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story ended the quarrels?
qa.a: Ammi's calendar with odd and even dates and a coloured mark for each job, because it made every turn visible.

qa.q: What was that first week like for the hamster?
qa.a: Unsettled: it was fed twice on one day and not at all on another.

grounding: An elder recalls two sisters taking alternate days to feed and clean a hamster and marking a calendar, which ended their arguments.

subtype: Approach: sharing pet duties fairly among siblings [Action]
passage: Kavitha and her younger sister Harini had shared Pista the hamster since March, and it had been one long argument. Then Kavitha had an idea: alternate days, marked on the kitchen calendar. K on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays; H on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays; Sundays together. It worked for a month. Then Harini left for a five-day school camp, Monday to Friday. "Who does my days?" she wailed at the door. Kavitha looked at the calendar. "I'll do them. You take the same number of mine when you're back." She crossed out the two H's that week and wrote K beside each, so there'd be no argument later. When Harini got home, she looked at the calendar, counted, and without being asked did Kavitha's next two days.

qa.q: What was Harini feeling at the door?
qa.a: Anxious about who would look after Pista on her days while she was away.

qa.q: What else could the sisters arrange for a longer trip?
qa.a: They could ask a parent to cover some days, so the whole load does not fall on one sister.

qa.q: How does the calendar help Kavitha?
qa.a: Kavitha can see exactly how many days she covered, so she is paid back fairly without a quarrel.

grounding: Two sisters share hamster care on alternate days marked on a calendar, which keeps things fair even when one goes away.
